newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU, Spain to meet on Telefonica, Unisource deal.
newsitem.headline: EU, Spain to meet on Telefonica, Unisource deal.

text.p: The European Commission and Spain will try on Wednesday to clear the obstacles to EU clearance of the Unisource telecoms alliance and Telefonica de Espana's participation in it.

Commission sources said Spain had informally proposed opening its telecommunications market to competition in January 1, 1998, at the same time as most of its European partners -- something Madrid has so far strongly resisted.
But the Spanish government must still commit itself to grant telecoms licences shortly after -- the only guarantee of effective liberalisation of the market, the sources added.
Spain proposed starting issuing licences in 1999, but this was "far too long", one source said.
Spanish Development Minister Rafael Arias Salgado, who is also responsible for the telecoms sector, was due to meet European Competition Commission Karel Van Miert in Brussels on Wednesday.

Van Miert has made it clear that unless the Spanish telecoms market is opened to fair competition in 1998, the Commission will not give its green light to the participation of partly state-controlled Telefonica in the Unisource deal.

The alliance was created in the early 90s between telecoms operators Dutch PTT, Telia AB of Sweden and Swiss Telecom PTT. Telefonica later took a 25-percent share in Unisource which provides value-added telecom services.
The Unisource agreement acquired a global dimension with the conclusion of a partnership with giant U.S. operator AT&T Corp , called Uniworld.
Like other transatlantic telecoms alliances, the Unisource deal is designed to take advantage of the break-up of national monopolies in Europe.
Other alliances are the Concert joint venture between British Telecommunications Plc and MCI and the Global One accord between France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom and Sprint Corp.
The aim is also to provide telecoms services to corporations on a global scale as the sector goes through a technological revolution providing countless business oportunities.

The Commission's demand that the Spanish telecoms market be fully opened to free competition in 1998 in return for clearing Unisource -- despite Madrid having negotiated in the past a five-year delay -- is no bold step. The French and German markets faced the same market opening requirements.
This must be seen also in the framework of global telecoms talks at the World Trade Organisation which negotiators hope to conclude early in 1997.
Spain is the only large EU country that has not yet committed itself to the 1998 deadline, provoking complaints from the United States.
